meta.title: Transfer Files from Phone to PC: 8 Ways, Wireless or USB (2026)
meta.description: Get photos, videos and files from an iPhone or Android onto Windows, Mac or Linux: Quick Share, Phone Link, AirDrop, a USB cable, iCloud or Google Photos, and a free app.

hero.title: Transfer files from phone to PC
hero.body: Pulling files off a phone sounds like one job, but it is really four: grabbing a couple of photos, emptying a camera roll, moving a video too big for chat apps, or saving a document you downloaded on the go. Each has a different best route, and the phone brand matters as much as the computer. Android phones reach Windows easily through Google and Microsoft, iPhones reach Macs through AirDrop, and the other combinations lean on cables, cloud libraries or a third-party app. Below are eight routes ranked, what each computer does with what arrives, the HEIC and Live Photo surprises Windows users hit, and where to look for the file afterwards. BIShare is one of the eight and the only one that sends from both iPhone and Android to any Windows, Mac or Linux machine across your Wi-Fi. Free, open source, no account.

updated: Updated September 2026 · Phone Link and Quick Share details from Microsoft and Google support pages, iPhone import steps from Apple Support
disclosure: BIShare is ours. Quick Share, Phone Link, AirDrop and iCloud are free and often already installed; for plenty of jobs below they are the right answer, and the page says which.

quick.title: Quick answer
items: Android phone to a Windows PC: share the file to Quick Share and pick the PC running Google's Quick Share app. It lands in Downloads, in a Quick Share folder.
iPhone to a Windows PC, photos: connect the cable, tap Trust, and import in the Windows Photos app, with Apple Devices installed. With iCloud Photos on, download the originals to the iPhone first.
iPhone to a Windows PC, other files: there is no general built-in wireless route yet. Use iCloud Drive or an app on both, such as BIShare.
iPhone, Pixel 9 or recent Galaxy to a Mac: AirDrop, with the Mac set to receive from everyone for Android. Files go to the Mac's Downloads folder.
Any phone to any computer on one Wi-Fi: BIShare on both moves originals directly, encrypted, whatever their size.
You are away from the computer: make a BIShare link on the phone and open it later in the computer's browser, within 24 hours, up to 100 GB.

types.title: What are you moving? That picks the route
types.body: The same phone can need three different methods in one afternoon. Match the job first, then the device pair.

0.h: A few photos or a screenshot
0.b: Speed matters more than volume, so the share sheet wins: Quick Share to a Windows PC, AirDrop to a Mac, Phone Link's photo gallery if it is already set up, or a direct send in BIShare. Chat apps work but shrink pictures unless you attach them as files.

1.b: Thousands of items favour a cable or a photo library. Import with the Windows Photos app, Image Capture or Photos on a Mac, or let iCloud Photos or Google Photos sync everything and download from the computer side. Wireless share sheets are tiring past a few hundred files.

2.b: Size caps decide it. Chat apps stop at 2 GB, Phone Link's drag and drop at 512 MB, and cloud libraries count against free storage. Direct routes, meaning Quick Share, AirDrop, a cable or BIShare on Wi-Fi, have no limit beyond free disk space.

3.b: PDFs, invoices and files saved from email are not in the camera roll, so photo tools will not see them. Use the phone's Files app with a share sheet route, a cloud drive, or BIShare, which reads from any folder the phone lets it open.

methods.title: Eight ways to get files off your phone, ranked

0.name: BIShare
0.tag: Best overall: iPhone or Android to Windows, Mac or Linux
0.facts: iPhone, Android, Windows, macOS, Linux · open source (MIT) · direct on one network, no size limit · links up to 100 GB for 24 hours · encrypted end to end · no sign-up
0.body: Open the app on the phone, choose photos, videos or files from any folder it can read, and pick the computer from the list of nearby devices; the computer accepts and the originals arrive at full size. Nothing about it changes between an iPhone and a Galaxy, or between a Windows tower and a Linux laptop, and it runs on a phone's own hotspot when there is no router. Leaving the house before the transfer is done is fine too: turn the selection into a link instead, and the computer downloads it in any browser later that day, with the file encrypted on the phone before it went anywhere.
0.cons: The direct route needs the desktop app installed. Links are gone after 24 hours, so they suit hand-overs, not archives.

1.name: Quick Share for Windows
1.tag: Best built-in route from an Android phone to a Windows PC
1.facts: Android 6.0 or later · a 64-bit PC with Windows 10 or newer, or Windows 11 on an Arm laptop · Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on both, within about 5 metres · files saved to Downloads › Quick Share
1.body: Once Google's Quick Share app is on the PC, it appears in the phone's normal Share menu under Quick Share. Tap it, accept on the PC if it is not set to your own devices, and the file is written to a Quick Share folder inside Downloads. It moves any file type the share sheet can hand over, including videos straight from the gallery, and Google publishes no size limit. Galaxy owners with a Samsung PC can use Samsung's version from the Microsoft Store instead.
1.cons: Android only. The two devices have to be near each other, and networks that block device-to-device traffic stop it; Google's advice is to join the PC to the phone's hotspot.

2.name: Phone Link
2.tag: Best for grabbing recent photos and screenshots on Windows
2.facts: Link to Windows on Android 10+ · Windows 10 or 11 · signed in with Microsoft · both on one Wi-Fi · shows the 2,000 most recent photos and screenshots · files saved to Downloads › Phone Link
2.body: Phone Link does two useful things for this job. Its Photos tab shows the latest 2,000 pictures and screenshots from the camera roll and screenshots folders, and any of them can be copied or saved to the PC in a click. For other files, share from the phone to Link to Windows, shown on some Samsung and Honor phones as Send to PC, and they arrive in a Phone Link folder inside Downloads. Phones with Link to Windows pre-installed can also drag files off the mirrored screen.
2.cons: The Photos tab shows images, not videos, and only from those two folders. Drag and drop tops out at 512 MB a file. The iPhone version handles messages and calls; Microsoft has so far offered iPhone file sharing to Insider builds only.

3.name: AirDrop
3.tag: Best built-in route to a Mac, from an iPhone or a supported Android phone
3.facts: iPhone, iPad to Mac · Pixel 9 and newer and selected Galaxy, Xiaomi, OnePlus and other models via Quick Share · nearby only · items saved to the Mac's Downloads folder
3.body: From an iPhone, tap Share, AirDrop and the Mac; if both use the same Apple Account it accepts without asking. From an Android phone on Google's AirDrop list, open Control Center on the Mac and allow AirDrop from everyone for ten minutes, then pick the Mac in Quick Share. Either way the connection is direct, the originals keep their quality, and what arrives sits in Downloads on the Mac rather than inside the Photos library.
3.cons: Mac only. Only a minority of Android models qualify so far, and the ten-minute Everyone window also lets strangers in range see the Mac.

4.name: A USB cable
4.tag: Best for a camera roll dump or a big Android folder
4.facts: Android: File transfer mode, any folder, File Explorer or a Linux file manager · iPhone: camera roll only, Windows Photos with Apple Devices installed, or Photos and Image Capture on a Mac · Mac to Android storage needs a third-party app
4.body: An Android phone set to File transfer in its USB notification shows up as a drive on Windows and in most Linux file managers, with every folder open for copying, not just pictures. An iPhone behaves like a camera: unlock it, tap Trust, and the Windows Photos app or Image Capture on a Mac can import photos and videos. Apple's note matters here: with iCloud Photos turned on, download the original full-resolution copies to the iPhone before importing, or the computer only sees what is stored locally.
4.cons: Nothing but photos and videos comes off an iPhone this way. Big imports over a USB 2.0 cable are slow, and on a Mac an Android phone needs a tool such as OpenMTP to browse its storage.

5.name: iCloud Photos or Google Photos
5.tag: Best when the whole library should end up on the computer and stay in sync
5.facts: iCloud: 5 GB free, iCloud for Windows shows iCloud Photos in File Explorer and Photos · Google Photos: 15 GB free shared with Gmail and Drive, download from photos.google.com · account on both sides
5.body: If the phone already backs up to a photo library, the pictures are on the computer the moment you sign in there. iCloud for Windows puts iCloud Photos into File Explorer and the Windows Photos app, and a Mac sees them in Photos. Google Photos works in any desktop browser, where you can download a single shot, an album or a selection as a zip. For documents, iCloud Drive and Google Drive do the same with the phone's Files app.
5.cons: It is upload first, download second, so a fresh batch of 4K video waits on your connection. Free tiers fill fast, and Google Photos only keeps full resolution when backups run at Original quality.

6.name: PairDrop
6.tag: Good when nothing can be installed on the computer
6.facts: Runs in any modern browser · open source (GPL-3.0) · finds devices on the same network · links devices on different networks through a 6-digit pairing code or a QR code · relays through a TURN server when a direct path fails
6.body: Open pairdrop.net in the phone's browser and on the computer, and on a shared network each shows the other straight away. Tap the computer, pick files, and they go peer to peer. It is handy on a work PC where you cannot install software, or on a friend's laptop for a one-off transfer, and paired devices remember each other.
6.cons: Both browser tabs must stay open while the transfer runs, large files depend on the phone not sleeping the browser, and there is no background transfer.

7.name: KDE Connect
7.tag: Best built-in route from an Android phone to Linux
7.facts: Android app with KDE Plasma, GSConnect on GNOME · Windows and macOS builds too · same network · also syncs clipboard and notifications · received files go to Downloads by default
7.body: Pair the KDE Connect app on the phone with the desktop once, and sharing a file to KDE Connect from any Android app sends it to the computer's Downloads folder. On GNOME the GSConnect extension speaks the same protocol. It is the natural choice for Linux users who want the phone and desktop to feel connected all day, not only for files.
7.cons: The iPhone app does far less than the Android one. Discovery can fail on networks that isolate devices, and it does not work outside the local network.

table.title: At a glance

rows.r1: Lands on Windows, Mac and Linux
rows.r3: Any file type, not only photos
rows.r5: Costs nothing and uses no cloud allowance

table.note: As of September 2026. For BIShare, the unlimited size applies when phone and computer share a network, while a link carries 100 GB at most. Google's Windows app only accepts files from Android phones and needs a 64-bit PC. Microsoft's app handles files for Android owners alone, wants a Microsoft account and one shared Wi-Fi, and rejects dragged files above 512 MB. AirDrop delivers to a Mac only, from an iPhone or from an Android phone on Google's AirDrop list. A USB cable gets any file off Android, but only photos and videos off an iPhone, and a Mac needs a third-party app to browse Android storage. Photo libraries eat into the free allowance, 5 GB at Apple and 15 GB at Google, and only hold pictures and clips; their Drive siblings take everything else.

windows.title: Android to Windows: Quick Share, Phone Link or a cable?
windows.body: All three are free and none needs a third-party app. The difference is what you are moving and whether you want the phone connected all the time.

0.b: Nothing to pair in advance and no published size cap. It is the quickest way to move a video from the gallery or a PDF from Downloads, and the file ends up in Downloads › Quick Share on the PC. Visibility set to Your devices skips the accept prompt when both are signed in to the same Google account.

1.h: Phone Link for photos you just took
1.b: Its Photos tab is the fastest route for a screenshot or a picture from a minute ago, because it is already showing the camera roll. Right-click a photo to copy it or save it. Shared files from the phone's share sheet go to Downloads › Phone Link, a folder you can change in Phone Link's settings.

2.h: A cable for everything at once
2.b: When the job is a whole DCIM folder or a phone's worth of WhatsApp media, a cable in File transfer mode lets File Explorer copy folders in one go, and it keeps working without Wi-Fi. For photos only, the PTP mode, often labelled Transferring images, lets the Windows Photos app import them like a camera.

iphone.title: iPhone to Windows: photos are easy, files are not
iphone.body: Windows treats an iPhone as a camera, not as storage. That makes photo imports simple and almost everything else awkward without the cloud or an app.

0.b: Apple's steps are to install Apple Devices from the Microsoft Store, connect the iPhone, unlock it and tap Trust, then import in the Windows Photos app. If iCloud Photos keeps optimised copies on the phone, download the originals first, or the import misses them.

1.h: The whole library: iCloud for Windows
1.b: Signing in to iCloud for Windows and turning on Photos brings iCloud Photos into File Explorer and the Windows Photos app, so new shots appear on the PC without a cable. It needs iCloud storage for the library, which for most camera rolls means paying beyond the free 5 GB.

2.h: Documents: iCloud Drive or an app
2.b: Files saved in the iPhone's Files app can be put in iCloud Drive and picked up from the iCloud Drive folder in File Explorer. Without iCloud, an app on both devices, BIShare or a browser tool such as PairDrop, is the practical wireless path. Phone Link's iPhone file sharing is still limited to Windows Insider builds.

maclinux.title: Phone to a Mac or a Linux computer
maclinux.body: Macs are easiest from an iPhone and Linux is easiest from Android, but both now have more crossover than they used to.

0.b: AirDrop for anything from one file to a few hundred photos. For a full camera roll, connect the cable and use Photos to import into the library or Image Capture to copy straight into a folder, which avoids filling the Photos library.

1.b: On a Pixel 9 or newer, or another phone on Google's AirDrop list, AirDrop to the Mac from Quick Share. Image Capture can also import photos from an Android phone connected in PTP mode. For other folders over a cable, a Mac needs OpenMTP or a similar tool, since Google no longer offers Android File Transfer.

2.b: KDE Connect or GSConnect is the everyday route from Android, and most desktop file managers mount an Android phone in File transfer mode over USB. iPhones are harder: file managers built on libimobiledevice can read the camera roll over a cable, and anything else is best sent with a cross-platform app or a browser link.

landing.title: Where the file lands on the computer
landing.body: Most "it never arrived" moments are a file sitting in a folder you did not expect. Check these first.

0.b: Quick Share saves to Downloads › Quick Share and Phone Link to Downloads › Phone Link. Photos imported with the Windows Photos app go to the Pictures folder unless you pick another. iCloud Photos from iCloud for Windows appear in File Explorer's navigation pane, and a browser download from a link goes to Downloads.

1.b: AirDrop puts everything in Downloads, photos included, so they are not added to the Photos library until you drag them in. Photos imports go into the library itself, while Image Capture writes to whichever folder you choose at the bottom of its window.

2.h: Linux, and anything received with BIShare
2.b: KDE Connect uses the home Downloads folder unless changed in its settings. BIShare on a computer saves received files to the folder set in the app, Downloads by default, and shows them in its inbox so you can open the folder in one click.

formats.title: HEIC, Live Photos and other files Windows trips on
formats.body: The transfer can succeed and the file still refuse to open. These are the usual culprits when an iPhone or Android phone meets a Windows PC.

0.b: iPhones shoot HEIC and HEVC by default. If Windows cannot open them, install Microsoft's HEIF Image Extensions and HEVC Video Extensions from the Microsoft Store, or set the iPhone's Settings, Camera, Formats to Most Compatible so new shots are JPEG and H.264.

1.h: Live Photos arrive in two parts
1.b: Imported over a cable, a Live Photo becomes a still image plus a short MOV file with a matching name. Deleting the MOV keeps the photo; keeping both preserves the motion, though Windows plays them as separate files.

2.h: Android motion photos stay in one file
2.b: On Samsung and Pixel phones the moving part of a motion photo is tucked inside the JPEG itself. Windows shows the still image; to keep the movement as a playable clip, export it as a video from the phone's gallery before sending.

0.h: Install on the phone and the computer
0.b: Install the phone app from the App Store or Google Play and the desktop app from the Microsoft Store, the Mac App Store or the Linux download. Join both to the same Wi-Fi or connect the computer to the phone's hotspot, and allow local network access on an iPhone when asked.

1.b: Choose photos, videos or files on the phone, choose the computer when it shows up and confirm on the computer. Originals arrive at full size in the receive folder.

2.h: Or send a link for later
2.b: Switch to Link, share the address to yourself, and open it on the computer whenever you sit down, within 24 hours. Nothing needs installing for that; the browser handles up to 100 GB.

speed.title: How long it takes
speed.body: The phone is the slow end of nearly every route here, both its Wi-Fi radio and, for cloud routes, the upload it has to finish first.

0.b: A current phone a room away from the router usually pushes somewhere between 40 and 50 MB/s over Wi-Fi 5, or 70 to 110 MB/s over Wi-Fi 6, which gets a 5 GB clip across in a minute or two. A phone hotspot is slower, often 10–30 MB/s.

1.b: A USB 2.0 cable caps out at 480 Mbit/s, and camera roll imports slow down further with thousands of small files. A USB-C cable and port that both support faster speeds help large videos more than photo libraries.

2.b: On mobile data or a slow upload, a day's photos can sit queued for a long time. A 50 Mbit/s uplink spends roughly three minutes on every gigabyte before the computer gets a chance to fetch it.

fixes.title: When the computer does not receive anything

0.h: The PC is missing from Quick Share
0.b: Open the Quick Share app on the PC so it is running, check that Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are on at both ends, and set the PC's visibility to Everyone for a test. Guest and office networks often isolate devices; putting the PC on the phone's hotspot gets around that.

1.h: Windows says the iPhone has no photos
1.b: Unlock the iPhone and tap Trust again, make sure Apple Devices is installed, and if iCloud Photos is on, download originals to the phone first. Photos stored only in iCloud are invisible to a cable import.

2.h: Android over USB shows an empty phone
2.b: The phone is in Charging only mode or locked. Unlock it, pull down the USB notice and switch it to File transfer. If the phone still looks empty, try a different cable, since many carry power only.

3.h: AirDrop from Android cannot find the Mac
3.b: Allow AirDrop from everyone on the Mac for ten minutes, keep its display on, and confirm the phone is on Google's supported list and updated. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi need to be on for both.

4.h: The photo copied but will not open
4.b: It is probably HEIC or HEVC. Install the HEIF and HEVC extensions from the Microsoft Store, or open the file in a viewer that supports HEIC, and switch the iPhone to Most Compatible for future shots.

security.title: Keeping the transfer private
security.body: Phones hold the most personal files anyone owns. How private a transfer is depends on whether the file ever sits on someone else's server.

0.b: A cable, Quick Share for Windows, AirDrop, KDE Connect and a local BIShare transfer never hand the file to a third machine, and every wireless one of them encrypts the link.

1.b: A BIShare link is sealed on the phone before it uploads, leaving the server with ciphertext it has no key for. PairDrop's WebRTC connections are encrypted too, even when a TURN server relays them.

2.b: iCloud Photos with standard data protection and Google Photos keep your library on their servers, where the provider can access it. Apple's Advanced Data Protection adds end-to-end encryption for iCloud Photos if you turn it on.

0.q: How do I transfer files from my phone to my PC without a USB cable?
0.a: Android owners on Windows have Google's Quick Share app and Microsoft's Phone Link. From an iPhone or a supported Android phone to a Mac, use AirDrop. For any phone and any computer, install BIShare on both and send over Wi-Fi, or make a link on the phone and open it on the computer.

1.q: Why does Windows only show photos when I plug in my iPhone?
1.a: Windows reads an iPhone as a camera, so only the camera roll is visible. Other files need iCloud Drive, an app on both devices, or Apple Devices for files inside apps that support File Sharing.

2.q: Where does Quick Share save files on Windows?
2.a: In a folder called Quick Share inside your Downloads folder.

3.q: Where does Phone Link save files on my PC?
3.a: Files shared from an Android phone to Phone Link are saved to Downloads › Phone Link by default. You can change the folder in Phone Link's settings.

4.q: Can Phone Link show videos from my phone?
4.a: No. Phone Link's Photos tab shows the 2,000 most recent photos and screenshots from the Camera Roll and Screenshots folders, and only images. Send videos with Quick Share, a cable or a direct app instead.

5.q: How do I import iPhone photos to a Windows PC?
5.a: Install Apple Devices from the Microsoft Store, connect the iPhone with a cable, unlock it and tap Trust, then import in the Windows Photos app. If iCloud Photos is on, download the originals to the iPhone before importing.

6.q: How do I send files from an Android phone to a Mac?
6.a: If the phone is one of the models that can AirDrop through Quick Share, let the Mac accept AirDrop from everyone for ten minutes, then choose it in Quick Share. Otherwise use BIShare or another cross-platform app, or import photos with Image Capture over a cable.

7.q: Why won't iPhone photos open on my PC?
7.a: They are usually HEIC images or HEVC videos. Install HEIF Image Extensions and HEVC Video Extensions from the Microsoft Store, or set the iPhone camera to Most Compatible to shoot JPEG and H.264.

8.q: What is the fastest way to move a big video from a phone to a computer?
8.a: A direct route on fast Wi-Fi or a good cable: BIShare on the same network, Quick Share to Windows, AirDrop to a Mac, or a USB-C cable. Cloud libraries and links are slower because the phone uploads first.

9.q: Is transferring files from a phone to a PC free?
9.a: Yes. BIShare, Quick Share for Windows, Phone Link, AirDrop, KDE Connect, PairDrop and a USB cable cost nothing. iCloud Photos and Google Photos are free until the library passes their free storage.

cta.title: From any phone to any computer
cta.body: Open source and free with no account. Send the originals across your Wi-Fi now, or a link you open at the desk later.

formats.title: Why a copied photo will not open on Windows
formats.sub: Three format surprises and the fix for each

a.fix: Install HEIF and HEVC extensions, or set Camera › Formats › Most Compatible

b.fix: Keep both files to keep the motion; delete the MOV to keep only the photo

c.fix: Export the clip as a video in the gallery before sending
